direction: Learn sparse, causally validated feature-level models of attention patterns ("routing features") to unfreeze attention in attribution graphs — the flagship circuit-tracing method's acknowledged weakest link.
project: Routing Features: Unfreezing Attention in Attribution Graphs
question: To what extent are attention patterns in a real LLM predicted by sparse interactions between interpretable upstream features at query and key positions — and can such a routing model replace frozen attention in attribution graphs without losing faithfulness?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B using the public transcoders (circuit-tracer) and Gemma Scope SAEs, compute pre-softmax attention logits for ~20 sampled heads (including known induction/name-mover heads) over ~10k diverse tokens, and regress logits onto (a) positional baselines and TAPPA-style query self-similarity, then (b) sparse additive query-side + key-side feature terms and low-rank bilinear interaction terms built from existing feature activations. Report held-out variance explained per head, labeling surviving interactions with automated interpretability. The falsifiable causal follow-up: for feature pairs predicted to gate routing (e.g., a duplicate-token feature boosting attention to earlier identical tokens), patch/ablate the feature and test whether observed Δlogits match the model's predictions. Success → rebuild attribution graphs with attention edges carrying explicit upstream feature causes, and measure gains in graph faithfulness (KL under replacement), the fraction of prompts with satisfying explanations, and a concrete proxy task: tracing which context token the model actually relied on.
why: It attacks a named limitation of the field's flagship tool, cited in both the Open Problems review and the circuit-tracing paper itself, that remains unfixed as of November 2026 — and the many 2026 attribution-graph papers (ADAG, annotation, decomposition, Circuit-Diff) all work downstream of frozen attention rather than on it. It is differentiated from the nearest neighbors: Lorsa interprets what attention units write, not why they route; the ICML 2026 QK covariance method is post-hoc and associational, with no causal validation and no tracing integration; TAPPA explains positional regularities, not content-causal routing. It is single-GPU feasible with existing open tools, produces a reusable artifact (per-head routing-feature models), and every outcome is informative: content features explaining logits upgrades the flagship interpretability pipeline for safety auditing; a negative result cleanly arbitrates, per head, between positional and content-causal theories of attention — resolving in empirical terms what is currently a standoff between TAPPA's positional account and the superposition hypothesis of attention.

direction: Mechanistically explain the "knowing–saying gap" — trace the readout/gating circuits that decide whether a language model's internally-represented error and uncertainty signals causally influence its outputs, or whether they are diagnostic epiphenomena.
project: Consulted or Ignored: Tracing the Readout Circuits of Hidden Error Signals in Language Models
question: When a transformer linearly encodes a high-fidelity internal signal that its current context is corrupted or its reasoning step is wrong, why does that signal fail to change behavior — which downstream components read the probe direction, where is the signal discarded or overridden, and what (e.g., a verification mode) switches the readout on?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, build the silently-corrupted-context multi-hop arithmetic task, train layer-wise linear probes to replicate the detection-vs-behavior dissociation (~0.95 AUROC vs. unchanged outputs), then measure the signal's causal connectivity component-by-component: subspace patching of only the probe-direction coordinates at each downstream attention head/MLP (per position, on-manifold, using causal head gating and edge attribution patching with integrated gradients) to see whether any component transmits the signal to the answer logits; then rerun the identical pipeline under an explicit verify-before-answer prompt — a condition where the model demonstrably acts on the signal — and diff the two circuits to isolate the gating components; finally, validate by intervening only at those gating points, testing whether targeted readout interventions convert detected-but-ignored errors into corrections without breaking correct traces, against the blunt-steering baselines that failed in prior work.
why: It converts a replicated, safety-critical empirical dissociation (probes see errors; behavior ignores them; all interventions documented to date failed) into the missing mechanistic explanation — something the three 2026 papers that established the phenomenon explicitly call for but none performed; it is high-leverage for safety (it determines whether probe-based monitors read causally engaged state or epiphenomenal summaries, whether self-correction is a prompting or a training problem, and it directly transfers to sandbagging/evaluation-awareness, the knowing-not-acting case), it is either/or decisive (a gating circuit enables targeted subspace interventions where blunt steering failed; proven inertness settles a contested assumption in the CoT-monitorability debate), and it has not been done because existing work stopped at documentation with whole-vector interventions (Yuan et al., Goel et al., Basu et al.) while the only circuit-level analyses in this space addressed different channels (verbalized confidence inflation, the known-unknowns hallucination feature), leaving the readout of the error signal into the answer pathway — the actual locus of the gap — untraced; it is also feasible now with open models and standard interpretability tooling, whereas competing frontier directions (weight-space decomposition, attribution-graph automation, developmental interpretability, SAE benchmarking) are already crowded by well-resourced groups in 2025–2026.

direction: Develop a causal-engagement framework that measures whether internal representations actually participate in producing behavior, validated across safety-relevant model organisms, to distinguish gated-but-present knowledge from truly absent knowledge and predict intervention efficacy.
project: From Presence to Engagement: A Causal-Engagement Framework for Internal Knowledge in Language Models
question: When a model's internals encode knowledge or capability that its behavior does not reflect (or reflects without the expected internal signature), what mechanism decouples them — and can a graded causal-engagement profile predict (1) intervention/steering efficacy, (2) elicitation cost of gated knowledge, and (3) the soundness of "absence" claims in safety audits?
first_experiment: Measure layer-by-layer engagement profiles (dose-response steering curves, controlled multi-direction ablation necessity tests with refit baselines, attribution-patching readout coupling, logit-lens tracing) for a panel of well-characterized latents across honest vs. gated vs. suppressed contexts in open-sourced organism models (secret-keeping, sandbagging-locked, unlearned, and control), then test whether these profiles quantitatively predict steering success, elicitation cost, and the gated-vs-absent distinction.
why: It targets the field's most repeated failure mode — misreading correlational presence (probes, SAE features) as causal use — which currently undermines SAE validity, steering actionability, monitor robustness under obfuscation, and the soundness of safety-case "absence" claims; it is unsolved because the relevant work is siloed (organism-specific causal models, application-focused elicitation benchmarks, metric critiques without replacements), the needed organisms and tooling only became openly available in 2025–2026, and no prior work unifies presence → engagement → actionability → audit soundness into one validated framework.

direction: Adjudicate the field's central contested hypothesis — that language models natively compute on superposed features — by building a ground-truth-anchored causal test battery and mapping the regime (width, feature count, sparsity, conjunction rarity) in which trained LMs use computation-in-superposition versus dense neuron-basis circuits, culminating in the first causal localization (or refutation) of computation-in-superposition in real language models.
project: In the Wild, In Superposition: A Ground-Truth Regime Map of Computation in Superposition in Language Models
question: When do trained transformers implement computation in superposition — computing functions of superposed features via linear readoff with feature-specific error correction — rather than dense neuron-basis circuits, and do the observed regime boundaries match theoretical predictions (Hänni et al. 2024; Adler & Shavit 2024; Ball & Box 2026)?
first_experiment: Train 1–2-layer transformers on a synthetic "superposed facts" language in which m binary attribute-features are frequent but their pairwise conjunctions are rare or held out, with inputs and outputs embedded via fixed random near-orthogonal directions; first validate a pre-registered five-test battery — (1) neuron-basis circuit sparsity via pre-down-projection activations and RelP attribution, (2) recovery of ε-linear readoff vectors for held-out conjunctions, (3) interference-scale analysis of virtual weights against the ~1/√d prediction, (4) the FSEC p-statistic and activation-plateau geometry, (5) error-correction-component ablation with selective degradation of conjunction readouts — against hand-planted U-AND and dense reference circuits, then sweep (d_model, m, sparsity, loss) and classify every trained run as CiS/dense/mixed to draw the regime map.
why: It targets the single empirical question on which the field's decomposition methodology and flagship safety applications (mechanistic anomaly detection, monitoring for hidden computation) currently hang; it is genuinely unresolved, with 2025–2026 results in direct contradiction (dense circuits, confounded toy models, aggregate perturbation evidence, and neuron-basis sparsity that is regime-limited) and no decisive causal test in a transformer with superposed I/O; it is decisive either way (first in-the-wild CiS circuit, or a legitimization of neuron-basis methodology); and it is not already done because the toy-model controversy over confounds was only settled in mid-2026, leaving the instrument (FSEC), the attribution tool (RelP/neuron-basis circuits), and the theory (U-AND thresholds) newly available but never combined — while big labs are occupied with scaling SAEs and interference-weight sparsification, and the controlled small-model training runs required are exactly what an independent researcher can execute.
